# Book I, Proposition 15

*Straight lines cutting one another make the vertical angles equal*

[Euclid's proof](#euclids-proof) · [In Lean](#in-lean) · [What it rests on](#what-it-rests-on) · [Mishnah](#mishnah)

> If two straight lines cut one another, they make the vertical angles equal to one another.

**In Lean:** ✅ proved, as Euclid states it · Euclid's argument

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/15-idea.svg" alt="When two straight lines cross, the angles opposite each other are equal: red matches red, and blue matches blue." width="420"></p>

<p align="center"><em>When two straight lines cross, the angles opposite each other are equal: red matches red, and blue matches blue.</em></p>

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/15.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition I.15, with Heath's letters" width="360"></p>

For let the straight lines AB, CD cut one another at the point E;

I say that the angle AEC is equal to the angle DEB,

and the angle CEB to the angle AED.

For, since the straight line AE stands on the straight line CD, making the angles CEA, AED,

the angles CEA, AED are equal to two right angles. [I. 13]

Again, since the straight line DE stands on the straight line AB, making the angles AED, DEB,

the angles AED, DEB are equal to two right angles. [I. 13]

But the angles CEA, AED were also proved equal to two right angles;

therefore the angles CEA, AED are equal to the angles AED, DEB. [Post. 4 and C.N. 1]

Let the angle AED be subtracted from each;

therefore the remaining angle CEA is equal to the remaining angle BED. [C.N. 3]

Similarly it can be proved that the angles CEB, DEA are also equal.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.

<a name="porism"></a>[PORISM. From this it is manifest that, if two straight lines cut one another, they will make the angles at the point of section equal to four right angles.]

<details><summary>Before the theorem, one lemma: <code>Prop15.figure</code> (26 lines)</summary>

```lean
/-! ## What Euclid reads off the figure -/

/-- Two straight lines that cut one another at E are two different straight
lines, so an end of one, other than E, is off the other. If E lies between A
and B and between C and D, and C is off the straight line AB, then A is
off CD and D is off AB. That is what I.13 asks when Euclid says that AE
"stands on" CD, and DE on AB.

Euclid's figure shows it at a glance. In Lean: a second point that AB and CD
shared besides E would make them one straight line (System E, Generalities 1),
and then C would be on AB. -/
theorem Prop15.figure {A B C D E : Point} (hAEB : Between A E B) (hCED : Between C E D)
    (hC : ¬ Collinear A B C) : Triangle C D A ∧ Triangle A B D := by
  obtain ⟨AB, hA_AB, hB_AB⟩ := Postulate1 A B (ne_of_between_ends hAEB)
  obtain ⟨CD, hC_CD, hD_CD⟩ := Postulate1 C D (ne_of_between_ends hCED)
  have hE_AB : OnLine E AB := on_line_of_between_ends hAEB hA_AB hB_AB
  have hE_CD : OnLine E CD := on_line_of_between_ends hCED hC_CD hD_CD
  have hC_AB : ¬ OnLine C AB := fun h => hC ⟨AB, hA_AB, hB_AB, h⟩
  /- The two straight lines meet only at E. -/
  have only_E : ∀ {P : Point}, P ≠ E → OnLine P AB → ¬ OnLine P CD := fun hPE hP_AB hP_CD =>
    hC_AB (line_unique hPE hP_CD hE_CD hP_AB hE_AB ▸ hC_CD)
  have hA_CD : ¬ OnLine A CD := only_E (ne_of_between hAEB) hA_AB
  have hD_AB : ¬ OnLine D AB := fun hD_AB =>
    only_E (ne_of_between (between_symm hCED)) hD_AB hD_CD
  exact ⟨Triangle.of_line hC_CD hD_CD (ne_of_between_ends hCED) hA_CD,
    Triangle.of_line hA_AB hB_AB (ne_of_between_ends hAEB) hD_AB⟩
```

</details>

```lean
/-- If two straight lines cut one another, they make the vertical angles equal to one another. -/
theorem Prop15 {A B C D E : Point} (hAEB : Between A E B) (hCED : Between C E D)
    (hC : ¬ Collinear A B C) :
    ∠ A E C = ∠ D E B ∧ ∠ C E B = ∠ A E D := by
  -- For let the straight lines AB, CD cut one another at the point E;
  /- That the two straight lines really cross, so that A is off CD and D is off
     AB, is what Euclid sees in his figure (`Prop15.figure`). -/
  obtain ⟨hCDA, hABD⟩ := Prop15.figure hAEB hCED hC
  have hA_E : A ≠ E := ne_of_between hAEB
  have hB_E : B ≠ E := ne_of_between (between_symm hAEB)
  have hC_E : C ≠ E := ne_of_between hCED
  have hD_E : D ≠ E := ne_of_between (between_symm hCED)
  -- I say that the angle AEC is equal to the angle DEB,
  -- and the angle CEB to the angle AED.
  -- For, since the straight line AE stands on the straight line CD, making the angles CEA,
  -- AED,
  -- the angles CEA, AED are equal to two right angles. [I. 13]
  have hCEA_AED : ∠ C E A + ∠ A E D = ∟ + ∟ := Prop13 hCED hCDA
  -- Again, since the straight line DE stands on the straight line AB, making the angles AED,
  -- DEB,
  -- the angles AED, DEB are equal to two right angles. [I. 13]
  have hAED_DEB : ∠ A E D + ∠ D E B = ∟ + ∟ := Prop13 hAEB hABD
  -- But the angles CEA, AED were also proved equal to two right angles;
  -- therefore the angles CEA, AED are equal to the angles AED, DEB. [Post. 4 and C.N. 1]
  /- Post. 4 has done its work already, as in I.11, so only C.N. 1 is left to
     cite. -/
  have hsums : ∠ C E A + ∠ A E D = ∠ A E D + ∠ D E B := CommonNotion1 hCEA_AED hAED_DEB
  -- Let the angle AED be subtracted from each;
  -- therefore the remaining angle CEA is equal to the remaining angle BED. [C.N. 3]
  /- The angle DEB is the angle BED, read the other way round (`angle_symm`). -/
  have hCEA_BED : ∠ C E A = ∠ B E D := by
    apply CommonNotion3 (c := ∠ A E D) (d := ∠ A E D) _ rfl
    rw [hsums, add_comm (∠ A E D), angle_symm hD_E hB_E]
  -- Similarly it can be proved that the angles CEB, DEA are also equal.
  /- Euclid's "similarly": this time CE stands on AB, making the angles AEC,
     CEB, which are equal to two right angles [I. 13]; so are the angles CEA,
     AED, as proved; and the angle AEC, which is the angle CEA, is subtracted
     from each [C.N. 1, C.N. 3]. -/
  have hAEC_CEB : ∠ A E C + ∠ C E B = ∟ + ∟ := Prop13 hAEB hC
  have hCEB_DEA : ∠ C E B = ∠ D E A := by
    apply CommonNotion3 (c := ∠ A E C) (d := ∠ C E A) _ (angle_symm hA_E hC_E)
    rw [add_comm (∠ C E B), hAEC_CEB, ← hCEA_AED, add_comm (∠ D E A), angle_symm hD_E hA_E]
  -- Therefore etc.
  /- Euclid's angles CEA and BED are the angles AEC and DEB of the enunciation,
     and DEA is AED, each read the other way round. -/
  exact ⟨by rw [angle_symm hA_E hC_E, hCEA_BED, angle_symm hB_E hD_E],
    by rw [hCEB_DEA, angle_symm hD_E hA_E]⟩
  -- Q. E. D.
  -- [PORISM. From this it is manifest that, if two straight lines cut one another, they will
  -- make the angles at the point of section equal to four right angles.]
  /- Heath, after Heiberg, brackets the Porism as probably not Euclid's, and the
     enunciation does not ask for it, so it is not part of `Prop15`. It is proved just
     below all the same, as `Prop15.porism`: the four angles at E are the two pairs
     that I.13 has just shown to be equal to two right angles each. -/
```

<details><summary>After the theorem, its porism, <code>Prop15.porism</code> (16 lines)</summary>

```lean
/-- The Porism to I.15: if two straight lines cut one another, the four angles at the point
of section, AEC, CEB, BED and DEA, are together equal to four right angles. It falls
out of I.13, used twice as in I.15 itself, with C.N. 2 to add the two pairs. -/
theorem Prop15.porism {A B C D E : Point} (hAEB : Between A E B) (hCED : Between C E D)
    (hC : ¬ Collinear A B C) :
    ∠ A E C + ∠ C E B + (∠ B E D + ∠ D E A) = ∟ + ∟ + (∟ + ∟) := by
  obtain ⟨-, hABD⟩ := Prop15.figure hAEB hCED hC
  have hA_E : A ≠ E := ne_of_between hAEB
  have hB_E : B ≠ E := ne_of_between (between_symm hAEB)
  have hD_E : D ≠ E := ne_of_between (between_symm hCED)
  /- CE stands on AB, and so does DE [I. 13]. -/
  have hAEC_CEB : ∠ A E C + ∠ C E B = ∟ + ∟ := Prop13 hAEB hC
  have hBED_DEA : ∠ B E D + ∠ D E A = ∟ + ∟ := by
    rw [add_comm (∠ B E D), angle_symm hD_E hA_E, angle_symm hB_E hD_E]
    exact Prop13 hAEB hABD
  exact CommonNotion2 hAEC_CEB hBED_DEA
```

</details>

**Reading the figure**

- [`between_cases`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L74): Of three different points on a straight line, one is between the other two. (Between 6)
- [`between_of_between_left`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L66): If B is between A and C, and D is between A and B, then D is between A and C. (Between 4)
- [`between_of_between_right`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L70): If B is between A and C, and C is between B and D, then B is between A and D. (Between 5)
- [`between_symm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L43) (used here): If B is between A and C, it is between C and A. (Between 1)
- [`centre_inside`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L35): The centre of a circle is inside it. (Generalities 3)
- [`circles_meet`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L201): If each circle passes through a point inside the other, the circles cut one another. This is the step Euclid takes for granted in I.1. (Intersection 5)
- [`circles_meet_same_side`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L81): Two circles that cut one another do so on each side of the straight line through their centres. (Intersections 8)
- [`exists_point`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L26): Let a point be taken. (Points 1)
- [`exists_point_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L38): Let a point be taken between B and C. (Points 3)
- [`line_circle_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L69): A straight line through a point B inside a circle, heading out to a point C outside it, cuts the circle between B and C. (Intersections 4)
- [`line_circle_beyond`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L75): A straight line through a point B inside a circle, produced beyond B away from C, cuts the circle there. (Intersections 5)
- [`line_unique`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L28) (used here): Two points determine a straight line. (Generalities 1)
- [`lines_meet_of_opposite_sides`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L179): A straight line joining points on opposite sides of L crosses L. (Intersection 1)
- [`ne_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L46) (used here): A point between two others differs from the first. (Between 1)
- [`ne_of_between_ends`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L49) (used here): The ends of a finite straight line differ. (Between 1)
- [`not_between_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L52): If B is between A and C, then A is not between B and C. (Between 1)
- [`not_between_of_between_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L79): If B is between A and C, and also between A and D, then B is not between C and D: C and D lie on the same side of B. (Between 7)
- [`not_on_line_of_same_side`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L92): Points on one side of a straight line are not on it. (Same side 3)
- [`on_line_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L56): A straight line through A and B, with B between A and C, passes through C. (Between 2)
- [`on_line_of_between_ends`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L61) (used here): A straight line through A and C passes through every point between them. (Between 3)
- [`pasch2`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L111): If B is between A and C, A is on L and B is off it, then B and C are on the same side of L: a straight line that leaves L at A does not cross it again. (Pasch 2)
- [`pasch3`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L114): A straight line through a point between A and C separates them. (Pasch 3)
- [`pasch4`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L119): If two different straight lines L and M meet at B, and A and C are points of M, different from each other and from B, that are not on the same side of L, then B is between A and C. (Pasch 4)
- [`same_side_or`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L99): A straight line has only two sides. (Same side 5)
- [`same_side_symm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L89): If A is on the same side of a straight line as B, then B is on the same side as A. (Same side 2)
- [`same_side_trans`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L96): Two points on the same side of a straight line as a third point are on the same side as each other. (Same side 4)
- [`triple_incidence1`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L131): Take B on L, C on M and D on N, three straight lines through A. If C lies within the angle BAD (on D's side of L and on B's side of N), then B and D are not on the same side of M: the straight line AC separates them. (Triple incidence 1)
- [`triple_incidence2`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L139): Take B on L, C on M and D on N, three straight lines through A, with B other than A and D off M. If C and D are on the same side of L, and B and D are not on the same side of M, then B and C are on the same side of N: C lies within the angle BAD. (Triple incidence 2)

**Superposition**

- [`superposition`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Superposition.lean#L30): **Superposition.** The triangle ABC can be applied to the straight line L with A on D, B on the ray from D through G, and C on the side of L where H is, without changing any side or angle.

**Laws of magnitude**

- [`add_assoc`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L23): Adding three magnitudes in a row, it makes no difference whether the first two or the last two are added first. (System E §3.5)
- [`add_comm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L26) (used here): The order of adding does not matter. (System E §3.5)
- [`add_lt_add_right`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L45): Adding the same thing to both sides keeps "less than". (System E §3.5)
- [`add_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L29): Adding nothing changes nothing. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_irrefl`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L32): No magnitude is less than itself. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_trans`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L35): What is less than the less is less still. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_trichotomy`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L39): Of two magnitudes, one is less, or they are equal, or the other is less. (System E §3.5)
- [`not_lt_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L42): Nothing is less than zero. (System E §3.5)

## Mishnah

_Our commentary: what Euclid assumes, what Lean made us say out loud, and how the result looks by modern means._

**Found by Thales, proved by Euclid.** Where two straight lines cross, the opposite angles are equal, and I.16 needs this at once. "This theorem, according to Eudemus, was first discovered by Thales, but found its scientific demonstration in Euclid (Proclus, p. 299, 3–6)" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 278). Where Heath's bracket gives [Post. 4 and C.N. 1], Common Notion 1 is enough for our proof, as in I.14.

**Why "vertical"?** Nothing to do with up and down. Two straight lines that cross, Proclus explains, "make two pairs of *vertical* angles (which are more clearly described as *vertically opposite* angles), and which are so called because their convergence is from opposite directions to one point (the intersection of the lines) as vertex (κορυφή)" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 278). Where one only meets the other, the angles are adjacent, as in I.14.

**Do the straight lines really cross?** Each use of I.13 needs a straight line standing on another, with its far end off it: A off CD, and D off AB. Euclid's figure shows it at a glance, and we prove it from the rule that two points fix one straight line. His "similarly" hides a third use of I.13, for the angles AEC, CEB, and there Common Notion 3 must be told that the angle AEC is the angle CEA.

**Is the Porism Euclid's?** Heath, after J. L. Heiberg, brackets it, weighing the manuscripts: "The balance of MS. authority seems to be against the genuineness of this *Porism*, but Proclus and Psellus both have it" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 278). A porism here is a corollary, "appearing as it were by chance without any additional labour, and constituting, as Proclus says, a sort of *windfall* (ἕρμαιον) and *bonus* (κέρδος)" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 278). Proclus says it underlies "that paradoxical theorem" of the Pythagoreans: of regular figures, only six equilateral triangles, four squares or three hexagons fill the space round a point (Heath, vol. 1, p. 279). We prove it apart from `Prop15`, as `Prop15.porism`, adding I.13's two pairs by Common Notion 2.

**The modern way.** Put E at the origin and A, C at vectors a, c, so that B and D lie along −a and −c: the cosine of the angle DEB is (−c)·(−a)/(|c||a|) = a·c/(|a||c|), the cosine of the angle AEC. In the complex plane, the half-turn z ↦ −z about E carries each angle onto the one opposite it.

## Further reading

- For the half-turn about E, which carries each angle onto the one vertically opposite it, George E. Martin's [*Transformation Geometry*](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4612-5680-9) (1982), ch. 3, "Translations and Halfturns", on the motions of the plane.
- For Thales, and Eudemus' history of the earliest Greek geometry, Thomas L. Heath's own [*A History of Greek Mathematics*](https://archive.org/details/cu31924008704219) (1921, free online), whose first volume runs from Thales to Euclid.
